Its main bodies are the General Assembly, where all members are represented, and the Security Council, which has five permanent members, the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France, with the power of veto, and ten rotating members. In 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

The UN also runs peacekeeping missions and agencies such as the World Health Organization, UNESCO and UNICEF. It has succeeded in some efforts and been limited in others. Azerbaijan became a member in 1992.

articles.title: The Cold War
articles.description: The rivalry between the USA and the Soviet Union.
articles.content:
The Cold War (about 1947–1991) was a long geopolitical rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their allies that never became a direct war between the two.

It was fought through an arms race, spying, propaganda, the space race and proxy wars such as those in Korea and Vietnam. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought the world close to nuclear war. Europe was divided by what Winston Churchill called an iron curtain, and Berlin was split by a wall from 1961.

The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, which ended the conflict. Azerbaijan restored its independence in the same year.

articles.title: Indian Independence
articles.description: The end of British rule in India in 1947.
articles.content:
India was ruled by Britain, first through the East India Company and, after the great rebellion of 1857, directly by the Crown. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, began to demand self-government, and the movement grew in the 20th century.

Mahatma Gandhi led campaigns of non-violent resistance, such as the Salt March of 1930, in which he walked about 390 kilometres to make salt in defiance of British law, and the Quit India movement of 1942. Other leaders included Jawaharlal Nehru, and Muhammad Ali Jinnah, who led the Muslim League in demanding a separate state.

Independence came on 15 August 1947, with the partition of British India into India and Pakistan. Partition caused mass migrations of about 15 million people and violence that killed perhaps one to two million. Gandhi was assassinated in 1948, and India adopted its constitution in 1950.

articles.title: The Korean War
articles.description: The war that divided the Korean Peninsula.
articles.content:
The Korean War (1950–1953) began when communist North Korea invaded South Korea on 25 June 1950. The peninsula had been divided at the 38th parallel after World War II, with the Soviet Union backing the North and the United States the South.

The United Nations sent forces, mostly American, to support South Korea. After landing at Inchon in September 1950, UN troops pushed deep into the North, but China entered the war in October and drove them back. The fighting settled near the 38th parallel.

An armistice was signed on 27 July 1953, but no peace treaty, so the two Koreas are technically still at war. A heavily fortified demilitarised zone separates them. Around three million people are thought to have died, and the war was one of the first big tests of the Cold War.

articles.title: The Vietnam War
articles.description: The long conflict in Southeast Asia, 1955–1975.
articles.content:
The Vietnam War (1955–1975) was fought between communist North Vietnam, led by Ho Chi Minh and supported by the Soviet Union and China, and South Vietnam, supported by the United States. It grew out of the struggle against French colonial rule that ended in 1954, after which Vietnam was divided.

American involvement escalated after the Gulf of Tonkin incident of 1964, and by 1968 more than half a million US troops were in Vietnam. The Tet Offensive of that year, though a military failure for the North, shook American public opinion. Bombing, the use of the chemical Agent Orange and guerrilla fighting caused enormous suffering.

The US withdrew its forces in 1973 under the Paris Peace Accords, and Saigon fell to the North on 30 April 1975. Vietnam was reunified in 1976. Perhaps one to three million Vietnamese and about 58,000 Americans died.

articles.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
articles.description: The 13 days when the world came closest to nuclear war.
articles.content:
The Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 was a confrontation between the United States and the Soviet Union over Soviet nuclear missiles secretly placed in Cuba, about 150 kilometres from Florida. It is regarded as the moment when the Cold War came closest to a nuclear war.

On 14 October an American U-2 spy plane photographed the missile sites. President John F. Kennedy announced a naval quarantine of Cuba on 22 October. For 13 days the world held its breath as ships approached the line and both sides prepared for war. A Soviet submarine officer, Vasily Arkhipov, is said to have helped prevent a nuclear torpedo launch.

The crisis ended when the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles in return for a US promise not to invade Cuba and, secretly, to withdraw US missiles from Turkey. A hotline between Washington and Moscow was set up in 1963.

articles.title: The Space Race
articles.description: The Cold War contest to reach space and the Moon.
articles.content:
The Space Race was a competition between the United States and the Soviet Union during the Cold War to achieve firsts in space exploration. It started on 4 October 1957, when the Soviets launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, shocking the West.

A month later the dog Laika became the first animal in orbit. NASA was created in 1958. On 12 April 1961 the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, and in 1963 Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman. In 1961 President Kennedy pledged to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out.

The US won the race to the Moon: on 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed with Apollo 11. The rivalry eased with the Apollo–Soyuz mission of 1975, and later cooperation led to the International Space Station.

articles.title: The Civil Rights Movement
articles.description: The struggle to end racial segregation in the United States.
articles.content:
The Civil Rights Movement was the campaign, mainly in the 1950s and 1960s, to end racial segregation and discrimination against African Americans in the United States. In much of the South, Black people were separated in schools, buses and restaurants and were blocked from voting.

In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled in Brown v. Board of Education that segregated schools were unconstitutional. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, which began a year-long bus boycott led by a young minister, Martin Luther King Jr. Protesters used non-violent methods such as sit-ins and marches, and faced violence.

At the March on Washington on 28 August 1963, King delivered his I Have a Dream speech. The movement won the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. King was assassinated in 1968.

articles.title: The Decolonisation of Africa
articles.description: How African nations won independence.
articles.content:
The decolonisation of Africa was the process by which African countries gained independence from European colonial rule, mostly between the 1950s and the 1970s. After World War II, European powers were weakened and nationalist movements grew stronger.

Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, was the first sub-Saharan country to become independent, in 1957. In 1960, known as the Year of Africa, seventeen countries won independence, including Nigeria, Senegal and the Belgian Congo. The British prime minister Harold Macmillan spoke of a wind of change blowing through the continent. Algeria won independence in 1962 after a bitter war with France, and Kenya in 1963.

Portugal's colonies, such as Angola and Mozambique, became independent in 1975, Zimbabwe in 1980, Namibia in 1990, and South Africa ended apartheid in 1994. The new states inherited colonial borders and economies, which have posed lasting challenges.

articles.title: The Soviet Union
articles.description: The communist superpower from 1922 to 1991.
articles.content:
The Soviet Union, or USSR, was a communist state that existed from 1922 to 1991, stretching across Eastern Europe and northern Asia. It grew out of the Russian Revolution and, at its largest, included 15 republics, among them Russia, Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.

Under Joseph Stalin, from the late 1920s to 1953, the country was rapidly industrialised, but the regime also carried out purges, forced collectivisation and imprisoned millions in the Gulag camps. In World War II, about 27 million Soviet citizens died, and the country emerged as a superpower rivalling the United States. It launched the first satellite in 1957 and the first person into space in 1961.

Later leaders included Khrushchev and Brezhnev. In the 1980s Mikhail Gorbachev introduced reforms called perestroika and glasnost, but they released forces that broke up the state. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December 1991, and the Soviet Union dissolved.

articles.title: The Fall of the Berlin Wall
articles.description: The moment that symbolised the end of the Cold War.
articles.content:
The Berlin Wall was built by communist East Germany in August 1961 to stop its citizens fleeing to the West, and it divided the city of Berlin for 28 years. The barrier, about 155 kilometres long around West Berlin, included concrete walls, watchtowers and guards with orders to shoot, and at least 140 people died trying to cross.

In 1989 change swept through Eastern Europe. Hungary opened its border in May, and East Germans poured out through it, and mass demonstrations in Leipzig demanded freedom. On the evening of 9 November 1989, an East German official mistakenly announced that the border was open, and thousands gathered at the crossings, and guards let them through.

People danced on the Wall and chipped away pieces. Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990. The fall of the Wall became the symbol of the end of the Cold War and of the collapse of communism in Europe.

articles.title: Azerbaijan's Restoration of Independence
articles.description: The path to independence in 1991.
articles.content:
In the late 1980s, under the Soviet reforms of glasnost, national movements grew in Azerbaijan. The Popular Front of Azerbaijan was founded in 1989. On the night of 19 to 20 January 1990, Soviet troops entered Baku, killing more than 130 civilians in an event called Black January, which turned public opinion firmly toward independence.

On 30 August 1991 the Supreme Soviet declared the restoration of independence, and on 18 October 1991 the Constitutional Act on the State Independence of the Republic of Azerbaijan was adopted. A referendum in December confirmed it, and in 1992 Azerbaijan joined the United Nations. In 1994 the government signed the so-called Contract of the Century with international oil companies.

The early years were hard, marked by economic crisis and by the conflict over Nagorno-Karabakh, which began in 1988. After a ceasefire in 1994 and fighting in 2020, Azerbaijan restored control over the region in 2023. Independence Day is celebrated on 18 October.

articles.title: The European Union
articles.description: The political and economic union of European countries.
articles.content:
The European Union (EU) is a political and economic union of 27 European countries. Its roots lie in the aftermath of World War II. On 9 May 1950, the French foreign minister Robert Schuman proposed pooling coal and steel production, so that war between France and Germany would be impossible. That day is now celebrated as Europe Day.

Six countries formed the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951 and the European Economic Community with the Treaty of Rome in 1957. The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 created the EU. The euro entered circulation as notes and coins in 2002, and in 2004 ten mostly Eastern European countries joined. Britain left in 2020.

The EU has a single market, in which people, goods, services and capital move freely, a Parliament elected by citizens, and the Schengen area without passport checks between most members. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012.

articles.title: The September 11 Attacks
articles.description: The 2001 terrorist attacks on the United States.
articles.content:
On the morning of 11 September 2001, 19 hijackers linked to the terrorist group al-Qaeda seized four passenger aeroplanes in the United States. Two were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed, and a third hit the Pentagon near Washington, D.C. The fourth, Flight 93, crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers tried to retake control.

Nearly 3,000 people were killed, making it the deadliest terrorist attack in history. The scenes were watched live around the world and shocked the public.

The United States responded with a global War on Terror, invading Afghanistan in October 2001, where al-Qaeda was based, and later Iraq in 2003. The attacks led to stronger security at airports, new laws such as the Patriot Act, and long debates about security, freedom and foreign policy.

articles.title: The Great Recession
articles.description: The global financial crisis of 2007–2009.
articles.content:
The Great Recession was a severe worldwide economic downturn that followed the global financial crisis of 2007–2008. It was the worst since the Great Depression.

Its roots lay in a housing bubble in the United States, fuelled by cheap loans, including risky subprime mortgages, which banks packaged into complex financial products sold around the world. When house prices fell, many borrowers could not pay, and banks suffered huge losses. On 15 September 2008 the investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed, and the financial system froze.

Governments rescued banks and stimulated the economy, but millions lost jobs and homes. A debt crisis in the eurozone followed from 2010. Regulations such as the Dodd–Frank Act were passed, and the anonymous inventor of Bitcoin launched that currency in 2009 partly as a response to distrust of banks.

articles.title: The COVID-19 Pandemic
articles.description: The global health crisis that began in 2019.
articles.content:
COVID-19 is an illness caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, first identified in the Chinese city of Wuhan in December 2019. It spread rapidly, and on 11 March 2020 the World Health Organization declared it a pandemic. Azerbaijan reported its first case in late February 2020.

Governments introduced lockdowns, travel restrictions, mask rules and closures of schools and businesses. Hospitals in many countries were overwhelmed. More than 7 million deaths were officially reported worldwide, though estimates of the true toll are higher. The economic effects were sharp, and many people shifted to working and studying online.

Vaccines were developed in record time, and the first were approved in December 2020. Vaccination campaigns and immunity from infection gradually reduced severe illness, and the WHO ended the global health emergency in May 2023. The pandemic changed attitudes to health, work and international cooperation.
